chapters.title: AI Foundations: Machine Learning for Space Engineers
chapters.scope:
- What AI is and is not: symbolic (rule-based, search, planning, expert systems, fuzzy logic) versus statistical/learned AI; why symbolic methods still matter in space (verifiability). A short history of AI in space: expert systems and schedulers of the 1980s–90s (e.g. NASA's CLIPS 1985, the SPIKE scheduler for Hubble — VERIFY), Deep Space 1 Remote Agent 1999 (mention only; details in Chapter 48), the deep-learning revolution (AlexNet 2012, transformers 2017, foundation models 2020s) and how each wave reached space. A computed timeline figure 1980–2026 of AI milestones in space.
- Problem types mapped to space examples (big table): classification, regression, semantic segmentation, object detection, forecasting, anomaly detection, clustering, dimensionality reduction, ranking, decision/control.
- Learning paradigms: supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, semi-supervised, active, transfer and reinforcement learning (RL only conceptually; applications in Chapter 48).
- The core mathematics in plain words: data, features, model, loss function, empirical risk; gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent with equations; backpropagation in one paragraph; regularisation; bias–variance trade-off; train/validation/test splits; cross-validation; hyper-parameter tuning; data leakage — especially the space-specific leakage caused by spatial and temporal autocorrelation (spatial-block and time-series splits).
- Classical machine learning, each with how it works and a space use: linear and logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, support vector machines, k-means, PCA, Gaussian processes; the Kalman filter as Bayesian estimation (link Chapter 6) and the relationship between estimation theory and ML.
- Evaluation: confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC and AUC, precision–recall curves, IoU, mAP, RMSE/MAE, forecast skill scores (CSI, Brier, TSS), calibration; class imbalance for rare events (fires, anomalies, conjunctions) and the accuracy paradox; statistical significance and confidence intervals on test metrics.
- Computed figures that actually run ML (numpy/scikit-learn): (1) gradient descent paths on a 2-D loss surface for different learning rates; (2) a small MLP written in numpy trained from scratch on synthetic 'cloud vs clear' two-band reflectance data — training and validation loss curves showing overfitting and early stopping; (3) decision boundaries of logistic regression, random forest and MLP on the same data; (4) ROC and precision–recall curves for a 1 %-prevalence detection task showing why accuracy misleads; (5) learning curve: test error vs training-set size; (6) k-means clustering and PCA of synthetic multispectral pixels; (7) random vs spatial-block cross-validation on a spatially autocorrelated synthetic field showing optimistic bias of random CV; plus a taxonomy diagram AI ⊃ ML ⊃ deep learning with space examples.
- Worked examples: precision, recall and F1 of a wildfire detector from a confusion matrix; one gradient-descent update by hand; estimating test-set size needed to measure a 1 % false-alarm rate with ±0.2 % confidence.
- Practice box: the end-to-end ML workflow for a space problem (define the decision, data, labels, baseline, split, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor).
- End with a road map of Chapters 44–53.

chapters.title: Deep Learning, Foundation Models and Generative AI
chapters.scope:
- Neural-network building blocks: neurons, activation functions, layers, backpropagation, optimisers (SGD with momentum, Adam), normalisation, dropout, initialisation; scaling laws (parameters, data and compute) in one section with a computed illustration.
- Convolutional networks: convolution, pooling, receptive field, residual networks; object detection (two-stage and one-stage/YOLO family), semantic segmentation (U-Net, DeepLab); computed figure: apply learned-style convolution filters (edge, texture) to a real NASA image and show feature maps.
- Sequence models for telemetry and time series: RNN, LSTM, GRU, temporal convolutional networks.
- Transformers: attention with its equation, multi-head attention, positional encoding, vision transformers and Swin, time-series transformers; computational cost (quadratic in sequence length); computed toy attention-weights figure produced by real numpy code.
- Graph neural networks: message passing; GraphCast's icosahedral mesh (applications in Chapter 47); constellations and networks as graphs.
- Generative models: autoencoders and VAEs, GANs, diffusion models (with the forward/reverse process equations) and flow matching; uses: super-resolution, synthetic training data, ensemble weather generation (GenCast — Chapter 47), design generation (Chapter 52); computed figure: a working 2-D toy diffusion model trained in numpy (or a simpler score-matching demo) showing samples emerging from noise.
- Self-supervised learning and foundation models: masked autoencoding and contrastive learning; embeddings, fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA), few-shot learning. Earth and space foundation models — build a verified table (developer, year, modality, size, training data, licence): e.g. NASA–IBM Prithvi-EO-1.0 (2023) and 2.0 (2024), Prithvi-WxC (2024), Clay, SatMAE, SkySense, ESA–IBM TerraMind (2025), Google DeepMind AlphaEarth Foundations (2025), Microsoft Aurora (Nature 2025), NASA–IBM heliophysics model Surya (2025) — VERIFY every entry.
- Large language models and agents: tokens, next-token prediction, pre-training, instruction tuning and RLHF, context windows, retrieval-augmented generation over technical documents, tool use and agents, multimodal models, code generation; hallucination and why it matters for engineering; space uses previewed (operations assistants Chapter 49, systems engineering Chapter 52, assurance Chapter 53).
- Physics-informed and hybrid ML: PINNs (residual loss equation), neural operators (Fourier neural operator), surrogates and emulators, differentiable simulation; computed figure: train a numpy neural surrogate of atmospheric density versus altitude (US Standard Atmosphere/exponential segments) or of the Planck function and compare error and speed with the physics model, including extrapolation failure outside the training range.
- Uncertainty quantification: aleatoric vs epistemic; deep ensembles, MC dropout, Bayesian NNs, conformal prediction — computed figure: conformal prediction intervals and ensemble spread on a regression problem with coverage check.
- Explainability: saliency, Grad-CAM, SHAP, feature attribution; limitations and misuse.
- Worked examples: parameters and FLOPs of a convolution layer and a small CNN; memory needed for a 7-billion-parameter LLM at 16, 8 and 4 bits; attention cost for an image split into 16×16 patches.
- Practice box: fine-tuning an Earth-observation foundation model for a new task with few labels.

chapters.title: Data, Computing Hardware and Edge AI in Orbit
chapters.scope:
- The data side: data volumes of space AI (Copernicus and NASA Earthdata archives, NISAR daily volume, Rubin Observatory nightly volume, telemetry archives — VERIFY numbers), data types (optical, SAR, hyperspectral, telemetry, spectra, light curves, text), labelling strategies (expert, crowdsourced, weak labels from OpenStreetMap and existing maps, active learning), analysis-ready and AI-ready data, FAIR principles, licensing.
- Benchmarks and datasets table (VERIFY): EuroSAT, BigEarthNet, SpaceNet, xView, fMoW, SEN12MS, So2Sat LCZ42, xBD, CloudSEN12; SPEED/SPEED+ (spacecraft pose); NASA SMAP/MSL telemetry anomaly dataset (Telemanom); ESA Anomaly Detection Benchmark ESA-ADB (2024); ESA Kelvins competitions; NASA Frontier Development Lab.
- Synthetic data and simulation: rendering, domain randomisation, digital twins, the sim-to-real gap.
- MLOps for space: data versioning, experiment tracking, model registries, validation gates, deployment, monitoring for drift, retraining; cloud platforms (Google Earth Engine, Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem, NASA Earthdata Cloud, AWS Open Data, Microsoft Planetary Computer — VERIFY current status); ground-segment GPU/TPU compute; block diagram of an end-to-end pipeline from satellite to model to user.
- Radiation and AI hardware: TID, displacement damage, single-event upsets, functional interrupts and latch-up; why weights and activations are vulnerable; mitigation (TMR, ECC, memory scrubbing, watchdogs, selective hardening, algorithm-based fault tolerance, redundant inference); radiation testing. Computed figure that really runs: inject random bit flips into the stored weights of a small numpy network trained on synthetic data and plot accuracy vs number of upsets for float32 and int8 storage, with and without ECC/TMR protection.
- Processors table (VERIFY, with year, power, performance, radiation approach): RAD750 and LEON-class baselines; Microchip PIC64-HPSC; AMD/Xilinx Versal AI Core space-grade; Intel Movidius Myriad 2 on Φ-sat-1 (2020) and Myriad X; Qualcomm Snapdragon on Ingenuity; NVIDIA Jetson-class modules on small satellites; Unibap iX-series; HPE Spaceborne Computer-2 on the ISS (2021); NVIDIA H100 on Starcloud-1 (Nov 2025); Google's radiation testing of TPUs for Project Suncatcher (2025); Chinese 'Three-Body Computing Constellation' (2025). Computed figure: performance-per-watt versus radiation tolerance (or versus year) from the table values.
- Model compression: quantisation (post-training and quantisation-aware), pruning, knowledge distillation, efficient architectures; computed figure that really runs: quantise the trained numpy network to 8, 6, 4 and 2 bits and plot accuracy and model size.
- On-board versus ground processing trade: downlink bottleneck — computed figure of data generated by imagers of different resolutions versus daily downlink capacity in X-, Ka-band and optical links; benefit of on-board cloud screening given that about two-thirds of the Earth is cloud-covered at any time (cite); latency, power, thermal and verification costs.
- Updating AI in orbit: uploading new models (Φ-sat-2 apps, ESA OPS-SAT 2019–24), software-defined payloads, split computing, federated learning across constellations (diagram).
- Space-based computing and orbital data centres: concepts and 2025–26 demonstrations (Starcloud, Suncatcher, Chinese computing constellations — VERIFY), physics of cooling — radiator area needed per kW at a given temperature — and economics.
- Worked examples: energy per inference for a CNN on a 5 W processor; model size after 8-bit quantisation; radiator area to reject 10 kW of compute heat at 300 K; downlink saved by cloud screening.
- Practice box: qualifying an AI payload for a small satellite.

chapters.title: AI for Earth Observation
chapters.scope:
- From pixels to information (link Chapter 13): scene classification, semantic segmentation (land cover), object detection (ships, aircraft, vehicles, buildings), instance segmentation, change detection (bi-temporal and dense time series), super-resolution and pan-sharpening, cloud and shadow masking, SAR-specific methods (deep despeckling, SAR ship detection, SAR–optical fusion and translation), hyperspectral unmixing and classification, crop classification from Sentinel-2 time series with temporal attention, 3-D reconstruction; table mapping tasks to architectures and metrics.
- Computed figures that really run: (1) a synthetic multispectral scene classified with a random forest and a small numpy CNN or MLP — classification map plus confusion matrix and per-class accuracy; (2) change detection by NDVI differencing vs a learned classifier on a synthetic before/after scene; (3) SAR speckle simulation and filtering (Lee filter vs a learned linear/denoising filter) with an equivalent-number-of-looks metric; (4) ship detection in synthetic SAR clutter: CFAR detector vs ML classifier with ROC curves; (5) value of onboard cloud screening/smart tasking (fraction of useful images vs cloud cover).
- Applications with verified case studies: agriculture (crop type, yield forecasting), forests and deforestation alerts (GLAD, RADD, Global Forest Watch), global land-cover products (ESA WorldCover, Google Dynamic World), building footprints (Microsoft and Google Open Buildings), mining and urban growth, water and wetlands; oceans and maritime (ship detection, 'dark' vessels — Global Fishing Watch Nature 2024 study, illegal fishing, oil spills, sea ice); disasters (flood mapping from Sentinel-1, Copernicus Emergency Management Service, the International Charter, damage assessment with xBD-trained models, wildfire detection — FireSat constellation and OroraTech, VERIFY 2025–26 status); greenhouse gases (methane plume detection and quantification with ML: UNEP MARS, Carbon Mapper/Tanager-1, GHGSat, EMIT, Sentinel-5P; MethaneSAT loss in 2025 — VERIFY); humanitarian and development uses (poverty mapping from night lights and imagery).
- Onboard EO AI: ESA Φ-sat-1 (2020) and Φ-sat-2 (2024) and their apps, CogniSAT-6 and NASA dynamic targeting demonstrations, Satellogic and Planet onboard processing, tip-and-cue and smart tasking of constellations (VERIFY each).
- The commercial EO analytics business and AI-ready products; geospatial foundation models in practice (link Chapter 44).
- Pitfalls: domain shift between sensors, regions and seasons; label noise; class imbalance; spatial autocorrelation in validation; geographic bias in training data; good-practice accuracy assessment (area-adjusted estimates, Olofsson et al. 2014); explainability; ethics and privacy of very-high-resolution imagery.
- Worked examples: images per day produced by a constellation versus analyst capacity; area mapped from one Sentinel-1 pass for flood mapping; methane emission rate from a plume using the integrated mass enhancement method with stated assumptions.
- Practice box: building a flood-mapping model from Sentinel-1.

chapters.title: AI for Weather, Climate and Space Weather
chapters.scope:
- Numerical weather prediction and data assimilation recap (link Chapter 16); ERA5 reanalysis as the training set (period, resolution, levels — VERIFY).
- The machine-learning weather revolution 2022–26 — verified table with developer, year, architecture, resolution, lead time, operational status: FourCastNet, Pangu-Weather, GraphCast, FengWu, FuXi, GenCast (diffusion ensemble), NeuralGCM (hybrid), Aurora, Prithvi-WxC, ECMWF AIFS Single (operational 25 Feb 2025) and AIFS ENS (1 Jul 2025), NOAA and other national centres' operational ML models, end-to-end systems learning directly from observations (e.g. Aardvark Weather) — VERIFY all statuses as of October 2026.
- How they work and are trained (autoregressive roll-out, loss weighting, graph meshes, diffusion for ensembles), how skill is measured (RMSE, anomaly correlation, CRPS, tropical-cyclone track errors), where they beat physics models and where they fall short (smoothing, extremes, physical consistency, dependence on physics-based analyses for initial conditions); compute and energy compared with traditional NWP.
- ML inside the observing and assimilation chain: satellite retrievals (precipitation from geostationary infrared, tropical-cyclone intensity), bias correction of radiances, fast observation operators, quality control; nowcasting (radar extrapolation, deep generative nowcasting, MetNet family).
- Computed figures that really run: (1) train a data-driven emulator (e.g. a small numpy neural network or linear regression on local stencils) of the chaotic Lorenz-96 model and compare forecast error growth against the true model with perturbed initial conditions and against persistence/climatology; (2) an ensemble of the learned model showing spread vs error; (3) nowcasting a synthetic advecting rain field by optical-flow extrapolation vs persistence — critical success index vs lead time; (4) a climate emulator: fit a statistical/ML emulator to a two-layer energy-balance model and test it on an unseen forcing scenario.
- Climate: emulators (e.g. ClimaX, ACE/ACE2 — VERIFY), statistical and generative downscaling, ESA Climate Change Initiative data, Earth-system digital twins (EU Destination Earth, NVIDIA Earth-2 — VERIFY), detecting and attributing extremes; caution about extrapolating learned models to unseen climates.
- Space weather: solar flare prediction from SDO/HMI magnetograms (true skill statistic), CME arrival-time prediction and its typical errors, geomagnetic index forecasting (Kp, Dst) with recurrent networks, NASA DAGGER (VERIFY), solar-wind and ionospheric TEC forecasting, radiation-belt forecasting, the NASA–IBM Surya heliophysics foundation model (2025 — VERIFY); operational adoption at NOAA SWPC, the Met Office and ESA (VERIFY). Computed figure: forecast a synthetic or real-statistics Kp/Dst-like time series with persistence vs a learned autoregressive model, with skill scores.
- Worked examples: true skill statistic from a flare-forecast contingency table; energy of one ML forecast vs one physics forecast with stated assumptions; how far ahead an L1 monitor plus ML can warn.
- Practice box: evaluating an ML weather model fairly against a physics-based baseline.

chapters.title: AI for Autonomy, Navigation and Robotics
chapters.scope:
- Why autonomy: light-time, contact gaps, constellation scale, cost and reaction time; ECSS autonomy levels (E1–E4 for execution, D1–D4 for data, F1–F2 for failures) in a table; computed figure of required autonomy level vs one-way light-time and contact fraction for representative missions.
- Architecture of an autonomous spacecraft: sense–plan–act, executives, model-based reasoning and diagnosis (Livingstone), behaviour trees, onboard FDIR; history and verified results of Deep Space 1 Remote Agent (1999), EO-1 Autonomous Sciencecraft (2004–17), CASPER, Mars 2020's onboard planner, ESA and CNES autonomy experiments (VERIFY).
- Onboard planning and scheduling: constraint-based and heuristic planners; computed figure that really runs: a toy observation-scheduling problem (power, data and visibility constraints) solved by greedy, randomised local search and exact/ILP-style optimisation, comparing value and run time.
- Navigation: optical navigation (DS1 AutoNav, Deep Impact), terrain-relative navigation (Mars 2020 Lander Vision System, SLIM, Chang'e hazard avoidance, SPLICE), crater detection with CNNs, small-body navigation (OSIRIS-REx Natural Feature Tracking, Hayabusa2), DART SMART Nav; computed figure that really runs: crater detection on a synthetic cratered surface with template matching vs a learned detector, and the resulting position fix error.
- Pose estimation of non-cooperative targets for rendezvous, inspection and servicing: keypoint CNNs plus PnP, the ESA–Stanford SPEC 2019 and 2021 challenges and the domain gap, lidar methods; computed figure: PnP pose error vs keypoint noise (numpy).
- Guidance and control: convex optimisation (G-FOLD, why it is not machine learning) versus learned policies; reinforcement learning for landing, docking and attitude control (research status, verification problems, runtime assurance/shielding); computed figure that really runs: train a simple RL or policy-search agent (numpy) on a 1-D or 2-D landing or attitude problem and compare it with a PD/LQR controller — learning curve and trajectories.
- Rendezvous, docking and proximity operations autonomy: ATV, Crew Dragon, Progress/Kurs, Shenzhou/Tianzhou, Orbital Express, MEV (link Chapter 40).
- Robotics: rover autonomy (AutoNav and ENav on Perseverance — distances and fraction driven autonomously, VERIFY), AEGIS autonomous targeting, robotic arms (Canadarm2, Dextre, Canadarm3 status — VERIFY), free-flyers (Astrobee), humanoids and dexterous robots (Robonaut 2, GITAI), multi-robot and swarm missions (NASA Starling, CADRE — VERIFY), formation flying (PRISMA, Proba-3), and constellation-level autonomy such as Starlink's autonomous collision avoidance (VERIFY numbers from FCC reports).
- Worked examples: how much autonomy a Mars rover needs with 20-minute light-time and one uplink per sol; collision-avoidance decision rate for a 10 000-satellite constellation; terrain-relative navigation accuracy from map resolution and image matching error.
- Practice box: designing and verifying an autonomy function with a runtime monitor.

chapters.title: AI for Mission Operations, Communications and Networks
chapters.scope:
- Mission operations today: control centres, flight dynamics, planning, telemetry volumes and parameter counts (VERIFY examples), and the operator-to-satellite ratio for large constellations.
- Telemetry monitoring, anomaly detection and prognostics on the ground: limit checking versus machine learning (Telemanom LSTM at JPL 2018, autoencoders, isolation forests, ESA's ESA-ADB benchmark 2024 and ESA/CNES/DLR operational tools — VERIFY), diagnosis and root-cause analysis, prognostics and health management (remaining useful life of batteries, reaction wheels). Computed figures that really run: (1) synthetic multichannel telemetry with injected point, contextual and drift anomalies — fixed thresholds vs a learned predictive (autoregressive or small numpy network) residual detector vs isolation forest (scikit-learn), with ROC curves; (2) the false-alarm budget for 10 000 channels as a function of threshold; (3) battery capacity-fade prognosis with uncertainty bands.
- Automation of operations: procedure automation and lights-out operations, ground digital twins, LLM-based operations assistants and copilots (verified 2024–26 deployments or trials at agencies and companies only), natural-language commanding and its risks, human factors (automation bias, trust calibration, skill fade).
- Scheduling and ground networks: DSN scheduling, ground-station-as-a-service, constellation contact planning; computed figure that really runs: scheduling contacts for many satellites over a few ground stations by greedy vs optimisation.
- Communications and networks: cognitive radio and spectrum sensing, signal and modulation classification with deep learning (RadioML-style), ML-driven adaptive coding and modulation, beam hopping and resource allocation in high-throughput and LEO systems (including reinforcement learning research), interference detection and geolocation, routing in laser-mesh constellations, network digital twins, AI-native 6G non-terrestrial networks. Computed figures that really run: (1) modulation classification of synthetic I/Q signals (features plus a classifier) — accuracy vs SNR; (2) shortest-path routing and resilience to link failures in a Walker-constellation laser mesh using networkx.
- Cybersecurity of ground segments and links with ML (intrusion detection, jamming and spoofing detection), link to Chapter 53 for adversarial threats.
- Worked examples: false alarms per day for 10 000 channels at a given per-channel false-alarm probability; operator workload saved by automated triage; throughput gain of adaptive coding and modulation over fixed coding.
- Practice box: deploying an anomaly-detection system in a control centre.

chapters.title: AI for Space Situational Awareness, Defence and Security
chapters.scope:
- Space situational awareness at scale (link Chapter 21): detection and tracking (streak detection in optical images, radar processing), data association and uncorrelated tracks, orbit determination and machine-learning correction of propagation errors (hybrid physics–ML), thermospheric density and drag forecasting with ML during storms, conjunction-assessment triage (ESA Kelvins Collision Avoidance Challenge 2019, ESA CREAM, operator practice — VERIFY), manoeuvre detection, object characterisation from light curves and radar cross-section, re-entry prediction, space-traffic coordination (TraCSS) and commercial SSA providers' use of AI (VERIFY claims).
- Computed figures that really run: (1) scaling of conjunction-screening workload with catalogue size and the effect of filters; (2) learning a correction to a simplified orbit propagator's along-track error growth vs a higher-fidelity reference (numpy); (3) manoeuvre detection in noisy residuals with CUSUM vs a learned classifier; (4) light-curve classification of synthetic stable vs tumbling objects with features plus a classifier; (5) streak detection in a synthetic star field by matched filtering.
- Defence and intelligence (open sources only, no operational detail): automated imagery exploitation and change detection at national scale (e.g. NGA's Maven Smart System — VERIFY public statements), activity-based intelligence, tip-and-cue across government and commercial constellations, signal and specific-emitter classification, missile-warning and tracking data processing (clutter suppression, track fusion; link Chapter 20), battle management and command-and-control (Golden Dome — VERIFY 2025–26 public facts), autonomy for rendezvous and proximity operations, counter-AI deception (decoys, camouflage), human–machine teaming.
- Law, ethics and policy: DoD Directive 3000.09 (2023), the Political Declaration on Responsible Military Use of AI and Autonomy (2023) and its endorsements, UN discussions on lethal autonomous weapons, NATO AI strategy, escalation risks and stability, export controls (VERIFY).
- Worked examples: daily screening workload for a 50 000-object catalogue; false alarms in automated change detection over a country at a given per-pixel false-alarm rate; probability-of-collision triage thresholds and manoeuvre numbers.
- Practice box: building a manoeuvre-detection pipeline.

chapters.title: AI for Space Science, Planetary Exploration and Human Spaceflight
chapters.scope:
- Astronomy and astrophysics: exoplanet discovery and vetting (AstroNet and Kepler-90i/80g in 2017, ExoMiner and validated TESS/Kepler planets — VERIFY counts), radial-velocity noise modelling, transient classification for the Rubin Observatory alert stream (survey start, alert rates and brokers — VERIFY), gravitational-lens finding in Euclid data (VERIFY), galaxy morphology (Galaxy Zoo and Zoobot), photometric redshifts, simulation-based inference in cosmology, gravitational-wave detection and parameter estimation with deep learning, radio transients (FRBs), JWST data reduction. Computed figures that really run: (1) a simulated transit light curve with noise and a box-least-squares search recovering period and depth; (2) photometric-redshift regression with a random forest on synthetic galaxy colours, or transient light-curve classification.
- Planetary science and exploration: crater detection and crater-count dating, boulder and landslide mapping, mineral mapping from hyperspectral data (spectral unmixing), fresh-impact discovery in Mars orbiter images (VERIFY 2020 result), plume and transient detection, landing-site hazard mapping and traverse planning, resource prospecting (link Chapter 41), onboard science autonomy (AEGIS — Chapter 48 — and PIXL adaptive sampling on Perseverance — VERIFY), sample curation (link Chapter 29). Computed figures: (1) crater size–frequency distribution from a synthetic detector with completeness correction and the resulting model age; (2) linear spectral unmixing of synthetic hyperspectral pixels.
- Heliophysics science uses not covered in Chapter 47 (feature detection, event catalogues).
- Human spaceflight: crew health monitoring and wearables, exploration medicine and clinical decision support for Mars-class missions, AI-guided ultrasound, behavioural health, AI assistants flown (CIMON on the ISS 2018–19; Callisto on Artemis I in 2022; later systems — VERIFY), intra-vehicular robots (Astrobee, Robonaut 2), predictive maintenance of life support and 'smart habitats', Earth-independent operations with long light-time delays, augmented reality for EVA and maintenance (link Chapter 33).
- Worked examples: transit signal-to-noise for an Earth-size planet; Rubin's nightly data and alert volume vs human vetting capacity; autonomy requirements for a Mars crew with 20-minute one-way delay.

chapters.title: AI in Spacecraft Design, Manufacturing, Launch and the Space Business
chapters.scope:
- Design: generative and evolutionary design (NASA ST5 evolved antenna 2006; NASA Goddard's evolved structures 2023–25; LEAP 71's computational engineering — VERIFY), topology optimisation — computed figure that really runs: a SIMP topology optimisation of a 2-D cantilever or bracket in numpy (with the compliance-convergence history), and the resulting mass saving; multidisciplinary design optimisation and trade-space exploration with surrogate models — computed figure that really runs: Bayesian optimisation with a Gaussian-process surrogate (scikit-learn) vs random search on a toy spacecraft design function; neural-operator and surrogate acceleration of CFD, thermal and structural analysis.
- AI-assisted systems engineering: language models for requirements quality checking, SysML v2 model generation, retrieval-augmented search of lessons-learned databases, test-case generation, code generation for flight and ground software, with verified agency/industry examples (VERIFY) and the risks.
- Manufacturing and test: additive-manufacturing process monitoring (melt-pool imaging, in-situ anomaly detection), X-ray CT and visual defect detection, composite and PCB inspection, test-data anomaly detection (vibration, thermal vacuum), mass production of satellites (VERIFY production rates), supply-chain risk analytics; computed figure that really runs: defect-detection classifier ROC and the cost-optimal threshold given costs of false negatives and false positives.
- Launch: why landing guidance is convex optimisation rather than learning; engine and vehicle health monitoring; launch weather and lightning prediction (link Chapter 37); range scheduling; autonomous flight safety systems (deterministic by design); trajectory optimisation.
- The space business: AI-driven analytics from satellite data (commodities, retail, finance), insurance (parametric products, risk models for launch and in-orbit failures), constellation design and capacity planning, spectrum management, customer analytics and pricing for satcom, AI companies in the space sector, investment trends (VERIFY 2024–26 figures and sources), and the new demand that AI creates for space (orbital data centres — Chapter 45).
- Worked examples: mass saving from topology optimisation; cost–benefit of an inspection model; number of expensive simulations saved by Bayesian optimisation.
- Practice box: introducing AI tools into a spacecraft design team safely.

chapters.title: Trustworthy AI for Space: Assurance, Security, Governance and Outlook
chapters.scope:
- Why machine learning is hard to assure: behaviour learned from data rather than specified, opacity, distribution shift, specification gaps; comparison with traditional software assurance (ECSS-E-ST-40C and ECSS-Q-ST-80C criticality categories, NASA NPR 7150.2 software classes, DO-178C).
- Standards and guidance landscape — verified table: ECSS-E-HB-40-02A Machine Learning Handbook (15 Nov 2024); EASA AI Roadmap and Concept Paper Issue 2 (2024); SAE G-34/EUROCAE WG-114 work (VERIFY status); ISO/IEC 22989, 23053, 23894, 42001, TR 24029 and TR 5469; NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (2023) and its generative-AI profile (2024); UL 4600 as an autonomy safety-case analogy; NASA AI guidance and governance (VERIFY).
- Assurance methods: operational design domains and data coverage, requirements for ML components, robustness testing (noise, corruptions, adversarial), formal verification of neural networks (bound propagation, SMT-based tools), runtime monitors and safety cages (simplex architecture), uncertainty-aware decisions, explainability as evidence, simulation-based V&V with scenario coverage, dataset documentation (datasheets, model cards), MLOps traceability, independent V&V. Computed figures that really run: (1) accuracy degradation of a classifier under distribution shift and sensor noise; (2) out-of-distribution detection with a Mahalanobis-distance runtime monitor — ROC; (3) interval bound propagation on a tiny ReLU network certifying a robustness radius; plus a simplex/safety-cage architecture diagram.
- Security: adversarial examples on imagery (computed figure: an FGSM-style attack on a logistic or small numpy network classifier, accuracy vs perturbation size), physical adversarial patches and camouflage, data poisoning and backdoors, model extraction and inversion, supply-chain risks of pre-trained models, LLM-specific risks (prompt injection, data leakage), cybersecurity of AI-enabled ground segments and spacecraft (Aerospace Corporation SPARTA framework, NIST IR 8401 — VERIFY), defences.
- Governance and ethics: EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) and its application timeline including any 2025–26 changes (VERIFY), US federal AI policy changes in 2025–26 (VERIFY), China's AI rules, UK approach, Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (2024), UN initiatives (Global Digital Compact, scientific panel and global dialogue — VERIFY), export controls on AI chips and space technology (VERIFY), space-agency responsible-AI principles (VERIFY), privacy, dual use, the environmental cost of computing, workforce and skills.
- Outlook to 2035, clearly separating facts from projections: foundation models for Earth and space, autonomous constellations, AI-designed spacecraft, human–AI teaming on the Moon and Mars, orbital computing, AI in servicing and assembly; open problems; a roadmap figure with confidence levels.
- Worked examples: energy and carbon to train a mid-size model with stated assumptions; number of test cases needed to demonstrate a failure probability below 10⁻⁴ with 95 % confidence; availability vs safety trade of a safety cage.
- Practice box: writing an assurance case for an onboard ML function.
- End Part XIII with a short synthesis of the eleven chapters.
